extracts titles of an opinion article from The Chronicle website: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} page <- read_html( width="70%"} ::: wooclap Put the following tasks in order to scrape data from a website: ::: wooclap-choices - Use the SelectorGadget identify tags for elements you want to grab - Use `read_html()` to read the page's source code into R - Use other functions from the **rvest** package to parse the elements you're interested in - Put the components together in a data frame (a tibble) and analyze it like you analyze any other data ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ![](images/13/wooclap-qr.png){width="200" fig-align="center" fig-alt="QR code for Wooclap"} Go to [wooclap.com](https://app.wooclap.com/OKZKXCY) and use the code OKZKXCY. ::: ::: ## A new R workflow {.smaller} - When working in a Quarto document, your analysis is re-run each time you knit - If web scraping in a Quarto document, you'd be re-scraping the data each time you knit, which is undesirable (and not *nice*)! - An alternative workflow: - Use an R script to save your code - Saving interim data scraped using the code in the script as CSV or RDS files - Use the saved data in your analysis in your Quarto document ## Where we left off... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|1-5|7-9|11-16|18-22|24-26|28-31|33-35|37-45|47-74|76-78"} # load packages ---------------------------------------------------------------- library(tidyverse) library(rvest) Article text ## Plan ::: incremental - Write a function that takes a URL and returns the article text on that page (then test it on a page) - Run the function on each page in the `chronicle` data frame (but start by testing it on a few pages) - Save the results in a new column in the `chronicle` data frame ::: ## Demo {.smaller} ::: demo - Go to your ae project in Positron. - If you haven't yet done so, make sure all of your changes up to this point are committed and pushed, i.e., there's nothing left in your source control pane. - Pull to get today's application exercise file: `ae-08-chronicle-scrape-II.R`. - Then, close your laptop, and watch me demo the next few step. ::: # The 🐘 in the room ## Go for it ask the question you want to ask!
::: {.question .fragment} If AI can do all of this, why do I need to learn how to do it myself? ::: ## Another demo ::: demo Let's try something simple... - Create a scatterplot of miles per gallon vs. displacement in mtcars, and overlay the best fit line for predicting mpg from displacement. - Now limit to cars with displacement below 200. ::: # Working with AI ## Codex as a coding collaborator {.smaller} Codex can... ::: incremental - Read the active file and related project files - Use existing functions and coding conventions - Edit files directly - Run code and report results - Revise its work after feedback ::: ::: {.question .fragment} Codex can take actions, but **you** define success and decide what evidence is sufficient. ::: ## Give it a concrete task {.smaller} > Use the `scrape_article()` function in `_ae-08-chronicle-scrape-II-A.R` to add a column to the `chronicle` data frame called article content with the content of the articles from each page. . . . Why is this a useful prompt? ::: incremental - Names the file and existing function - Names the data frame - Describes the desired output - Provides enough context to inspect the project ::: ## Inspect the generated code {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chronicle <- chronicle |> mutate(article_content = map_chr(url, scrape_article)) ``` ::: . . . `map_chr()` applies `scrape_article()` to every URL and requires the function to return one character value per row. ::: {.question .fragment} Is generating syntactically valid code enough? ::: ## Writing code $\neq$ verifying code {.smaller} > **Human:** Did you run this code to confirm it works? > **Codex:** No. I only confirmed that the script parses without syntax errors. . . . ::: columns ::: {.column width="33%"} **Parsing** Is the syntax valid? ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Execution** Does the code run? ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Validation** Is the output correct? ::: ::: ## Test small before scaling up {.smaller} > Try it with the first three rows of the data frame to test if it works. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chronicle_test <- chronicle |> slice_head(n = 3) |> mutate( article_content = map_chr(url, scrape_article) ) chronicle_test |> transmute( title, content_chars = str_length(article_content), preview = str_trunc(article_content, 100) ) ``` ::: ## Ask for evidence in the prompt {.smaller} **Basic:** > Add the article content column. . . . **Better:** > Use `scrape_article()` to add an `article_content` column to `chronicle`. Test it on the first three rows before running it on the complete data. Confirm that the results are non-missing and non-empty. Do not overwrite the CSV during the test. . . . ::: {.question} **Context + task + constraints + verification + reporting** ::: ## The human remains responsible {.smaller} You need enough knowledge to... ::: incremental - Describe the intended computation - Understand and inspect the generated code - Design a meaningful test - Recognize implausible output - Diagnose failures - Consider responsible scraping practices - Decide when the evidence is strong enough to proceed ::: ::: {.question .fragment} AI can produce code quickly. Statistical and computational knowledge lets you decide whether that code answers the right question -- and whether it actually works. ::: ## How does Codex know how to work? {.smaller} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ### `AGENTS.md` - Persistent instructions for a repository - Describes project conventions, expectations, and checks - Read by Codex before it begins working **How to work in this project** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Skills - Reusable instructions for a particular kind of task - Loaded when requested or when the task matches - Can include scripts, references, and assets **How to do this kind of task** ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} Homework and lab repositories in this class, as well as the course project, use `AGENTS.md` files. Codex reads them -- and you should too! ::: [`AGENTS.md` documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md) · [Skills documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
